However, the relative recency of tensor classification as a machine learning application has meant that introductory resources in this field have historically been limited. In this paper, we explore how tensors are classified through machine learning and then calculate a similarity score between two tensors. We also recognize that there are various ways to classify objects, particularly in computer vision, and propose a novel approach for classifying tensors based on their visual representation. Like classification, this method involves assigning a single label to a tensor, but it can also measure the likelihood that a tensor belongs to each class. We illustrate the potential of this method by utilizing it to analyze a dataset of 35,000 handshakes from the EMCL Handshake Dataset. To facilitate further research, we have created an open-source project that enables users to create and train their own models for classifying and analyzing 3D tensors. This project is available at https://github.com/jamesbradbury/tensor-classification. We have also released a Python library called Handshake-Tensor-Classification, which provides a simple interface for classifying and analyzing tensors. This is the first comprehensive introduction to classifying and analyzing tensors through machine learning, and it demonstrates the feasibility of this approach through both a classification model and a novel approach for assigning labels to tensors based on their visual representation. In complex structures, the underlying cause of this vibrational behavior can be difficult to decipher from the resulting time-series data collected from the system. To address this challenge, this work introduces a cutting-edge data-driven framework that simultaneously identifies the parameters governing a system's dynamics and the corresponding mode shapes responsible for observed oscillations. Our bounding box prediction tool (BBox-PT) offers a user-friendly interface that allows even those without prior experience to easily label boxes and fine-tune detection models. We provide a comprehensive overview of the tools' key features and functionalities, along with a detailed examination of the system's architecture and a description of the development process. Additionally, we include a simple example of the tools' implementation and a brief discussion of our current limitations and plans for future improvement. BBox-PT is currently available for download on the open-source platform GitHub, with the aim of enabling its further modification and expansion for personal use. By sharing our implementation, we hope to contribute to the existing body of research and support the ongoing development of truly open and accessible image annotation software. Currently, the BBox-PT tool has been officially released for use in the datasets of the Traffic Sign 4F, Cars11, and Stomacher Challenge, with the aim of gathering user feedback and incorporating community input to further enhance and refine the software. Although primarily designed for a general research audience, BBox-PT's user-friendly interface and open-source code make it a viable option for teaching and training students in the field of deep learning. By utilizing our tool, students can focus on mastering the underlying concepts and techniques of deep learning without being hindered by complicated annotation software. One potential application of BBox-PT is in its compatibility with fully convolutional object detection models, which can be downloaded from various open-source repositories and integrated with the annotated data to produce high-performing results. Furthermore, to further streamline the data preparation process, we have developed a Python function to split and organize image data from a specified folder, with the option to include predefined classes and use BBox-PT's'mass labeling' feature to annotate a random selection of images. Similarly, we have created a Python script to extract and save the annotated data from BBox-PT's output, with the aim of producing results in a format compatible with various deep learning frameworks. Although primarily designed to support the development of object detection models, the tools' annotated bounding box data can also be utilized in a range of applications, including further research into visual perception in humans and animals. However, it is currently unclear if these GAN-generated simulations are suitable for use in policy assessments. To address this, we used Alabama's public school system as our study area and ran policy scenarios through both actual epidemic models and the synthesized datasets produced by different GAN methods. We discovered that the simulated data were highly susceptible to outliers and that the fit of the GAN-generated simulations varied greatly from one region to another within the same dataset. Furthermore, we found that the synthetic data were unable to replicate the spatial patterns of the original data in some cases, which resulted in inconsistent predictions in the application scenarios. Based on our results, we recommend using alternative techniques such as progressive GANs, especially the PGAN method, which produces more consistent simulations that capture both the overall and local temporal patterns of the original data. When combined with superconductivity, a versatile device can be created that rapidly switches between a resonant telegraph signal and a current blockade. This SET-Superconducting loop (NS) system develops distinctively strong electron spin interactions due to their proximity to the Shottky barrier. When subjected to microwave pulses, the NS-SET can effectively absorb and convert electrons, marking the beginning of spin-based quantum information in semiconductors. In this work, the incorporation of in-plane spin injection into a quantum dot formed at the NS-SET's boundary is investigated. Prior to the injection, the magnetic field is optimized to create a near-lateral electric field, which controls the magnetic interaction between the injected spin and the target spin. Additionally, a description of the spin and charge dynamics within the system is developed, as well as the conditions necessary to observe Coulomb blockade, telegraph signal, and a spin-blockade effect. Ultimately, this research provides the theoretical groundwork for the integration of spin-based principles into a quantum information architecture. In particular, the use of SETs in conjunction with spin-based principles may facilitate the implementation of quantum gates such as the single-qubit gate inspired by the orientation of electron spin (QUEOS) and the two-qubit gate controlled by the correlated exchange interaction (CET). As such, the presence of quantum dots at the boundary of the SET-SO system may become an essential component in quantum information technology in the future. In a related context, the potential existence of spin-blockade in the SET-SO system could also be leveraged in searching for dark matter. Lastly, the possibility of scaling up this device, with multiple SETs in parallel, is explored. Such a parallel-SET structure may offer a macroscopic means to observe low-energy spin-dependent interactions with unusual origin (LESDA), which could potentially facilitate the direct search for LESDA. As an additional advantage, the parallel-SET system may also enable the realization of multi-qubit logic gates, which could mark an important milestone in the development of quantum information technology in the future. A new study focuses on developing a quantum processor for linear algebra.  It employs a physically realistic model of a coupled-qubit lattice to investigate quantum computation.  The processor features two types of defects: vacancy defects with localized spins that can be used as single-qubit gates, and rattling atoms that enable two-qubit coupling.  The analysis includes temperature effects by considering spin relaxation and atomic vibrations.  The study initially identifies and eliminates defect categories that do not support quantum computation.  It then optimizes defect placement and coupling to achieve highest accuracy in quantum computation.  The study confirms the feasibility of achieving fault-tolerant quantum computation at room temperature.  It also suggests the use of Mo-based graphene as the most realistic model to date for quantum processing in two-dimensional materials.  The study further proposes that Mo-based graphene can be used to develop efficient quantum processors for linear algebra.  The outcomes of this research are highly relevant to current experiments and offer realistic guidelines for future studies on quantum processing in two-dimensional materials.  They are particularly valuable for experiments using Mo-based graphene, which has been extensively studied and offers great potential for further investigation.  The study finally discusses the limitations and difficulties that arise when implementing quantum processing in two-dimensional materials in real-world scenarios.  It is our hope that this study inspires the development of novel techniques to overcome these challenges and improve the efficiency of quantum processing in two-dimensional materials. At its core, storytelling is an intricate web of cognitive, emotional, and cultural interconnections that have significantly influenced its development and impact on society. Recent breakthroughs in processing and context representation have enabled machine learning models to mimic the storytelling process, which has sparked both wonder and concern. While these digital models emulate stories, they necessarily lack the cultural context required to truly convey meaning. In this study, we explore the boundaries between human and computational narrative generation and examine the stories that machines can create to communicate with us. To initiate this investigation, we designed and executed surveys to determine what people think is essential for a machine to effectively tell a story. The results showed that the public's answer to this question was surprisingly diverse and open-ended. Next, we utilized these findings to craft a set of questions aimed at assessing the ability of state-of-the-art language models to create engaging stories. Our experiments revealed that these models can successfully generate stories that align with human values, but tend to produce narratives that are often fictional and occasionally inaccurate. Lastly, we used the public's input to develop a new evaluation metric called Value-Constrained Story Generation, which evaluates the ability of computational models to create morally responsible stories. The outcomes of this study show that while computers can create extensive collections of stories, these narratives lack the cultural significance and emotional resonance required to truly connect with humanity. The public's input has played a pivotal role in illuminating the meaning and purpose behind these digital stories, which in turn has exposed the limitations of these models from a computational perspective. Ultimately, this research marks the beginning of an interdisciplinary investigation into the relationships between human and computational narrative generation. The insights gained from this study will be made publicly available to foster a deeper understanding of the stories that machines can effectively tell. The source code for the models will be shared on GitHub, and the results of the surveys, experiments, and novel metric developed in this research will be deposited at the arXiv repository for future access. Finally, we invite various stakeholders to engage in further discussion about the implications of this research through the Curves in AI repository. Our goal is to facilitate an open and collaborative exploration of the boundaries between human and computational narrative generation, which we believe is a promising area of research that requires rigorous scrutiny and debate. In the spirit of transparency and openness, we have designed our study to be easily replicable and extendable. We look forward to incorporating the public's input into our findings and trust that this research will inspire a new wave of studies in this field.

networks, including how they fit learning data and make predictions, remains a pressing issue in AI research. From a mathematical standpoint, studying neural network learning is complex due to the network's intricate structure and non-smooth outputs. Nevertheless, researchers have made significant progress in framing these challenges as optimization problems that can be explored using approximation techniques, such as ordinariness. This paper examines the foundations of ordinariness in neural networks, demonstrating under what conditions it applies, and provides explicit criteria for identifying regions of application. Furthermore, we investigate the generalized Taylor series, initially proposed as an approximation tool for neural network derivatives, demonstrating its utility for studying neural network learning via ordinariness. An analysis of our findings within the context of artificial neural networks reveals some intriguing results, including the confirmation of ourordinariness criteria through direct verification of the generalized Taylor series conditions. Also, through the local Taylor expansion, we prove that in many simple feedforward networks, the learning loss is consistently smooth throughout the optimization process. This result explains why such networks can sometimes exhibit previously unknown behaviors, such as sudden drops in performance, as observed in recent research. Overall, our study marks a new milestone in AI research, namely a rigorous exchange between neural network mathematics and deep learning practice. This work is heavily inspired by and has been reviewed for consistency with the traditional Taylor series and its applications in complex function analysis, as established by Lagrange and Cauchy. Moreover, we have prepared an extension of our findings to other neural network architectures, as presented in the companion paper (2022). Lastly, this research has also been made available under an open-access license, providing a transparent case study in AI mathematics. The associated code can be found here: https://github.com/jorgepgoncalves/neuronal_ordinariness. The computational simulations referred to in this research can be accessed at: https://github.com/jorgepgoncalves/taylor_series_in_neural_networks. Additionally, the corresponding mathematical paper is titled `Ordinariness in Neural Networks: Characterization, Approximations, and Applications,' and can be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.10777. The AI mathematics companion paper is titled `Neural Network Mathematics: Taylor & Fourier in Artificial Intelligence,' and can be accessed at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.10776. Lastly, this research has also been shared on the corresponding author's blog at: https://jorgepgoncalves.github.io/2022-03-21

To tackle this challenge, most existing solutions rely on hierarchical representations of text, building upon and refining lower-level details. However, current techniques often struggle to balance these relationships due to limitations in their architectural designs. This study proposes a simple yet effective way to learn hierarchical representations of text: using a type of soft attention mechanism within a recurrent neural network. Graph data often consists of various attributes that provide valuable information about the structured data, yet prior studies have not fully leveraged these attributes due to their rigid data models. To overcome this limitation, we developed the attribute-aware subgraph summarization framework, Asumu, which efficiently summarizes multiple subgraphs based on shared structural patterns and attributes. To optimize the subgraph summarization problem, we modified the maximum coverage problem and proposed an algorithm with two variants: the exact algorithm for exact matches and heuristic algorithms for metric learning. The initial wavepacket of electrons in the ions is generated by the laser field, and the time delay in ionization occurs when the wavepacket components reach the ionizing threshold. The process is evaluated under two extreme conditions: when the wavepacket amplitudes are extremely high and extremely low. When the wavepacket has an extremely high amplitude, it decays before reaching the threshold, resulting in a delayed ionization; in contrast, a wavepacket with an extremely low amplitude fails to decay and thus reaches the threshold first, leading to an accelerated ionization process. The time delays are significantly influenced by the square of the wavepacket amplitude to energy ratio, and they increase significantly as the ion charge increases. Initially, we adapt and evaluate a conventional multigrid method on a test case involving stationary electric fields. Subsequently, we apply it to a dynamic magnetic reconnection scenario featuring Alfv\'en wave propagation. By utilizing a V-cycle technique with seven grid refinements, we achieve a significant reduction in the time step limit imposed by the finite difference method, amounting to a roughly sevenfold increase. Our simulations indicate that the PIP model yields accurate reconnection efficiency values and Alfv\'en wave spectra consistent with precisely kinetic Alfv\'en wave theory. Furthermore, we obtain reconnection efficiency rates comparable to full particle-in-cell simulations and one-dimensional reduced MHD models. However, the efficiency rates in the PIP model exhibit a mild dependence on the grid resolution until reaching seven grid refinements. Eventually, we isolate the source of the time step limitation in the PIP model as resulting from the finite difference approximation of the magnetic advection differential equation. Our proposed solver essentially treats this differential equation as a nonlinear transport process, enabling the time step limit to be similar to that in full particle-in-cell simulations. By achieving this, the multigrid solver enables efficient modeling of reconnection efficiency and Alfv\'en wave dynamics within the approximately kinetic Alfv\'en wave regime, even on a wide range of timescales. Nonetheless, the solver's performance in the non-resonant diffusion regime remains to be explored in future studies. Ultimately, our work facilitates the use of the PIP model for Alfv\'en wave turbulence and radiation studies in various astrophysical settings. Our obtained solution procedures are also applicable to integrating the electric field via the finite difference method, potentially enabling more accurate results in future investigations. For instance, we could obtain reconnection efficiency rates comparable to full particle-in-cell simulations and one-dimensional reduced MHD models, simply by matching the electric field time evolution to the magnetic field evolution time using the finite difference method. Our solution in the PIP model bears some resemblance to integrating electric field via the finite element method in the electron fluid model (B\"uchner, 1996). Our proposed general solution strategy in the PIP model is to integrate electric field via the finite element method in a future investigation. In order to properly analyze this phenomenon, we have developed a novel approach that allows for the extraction of information from noisy data. This method is based on the principle of maximum entropy production and in the context of the Hodgkin-Huxley model, it has enabled the determination of the most likely distribution of currents across the cell membrane. Our results demonstrate that the maximum entropy production approach can effectively extract meaningful information from noisy data and may have far-reaching applications in the study of complex biological systems. In particular, this method offers a promising solution to the issue of extracting information from stochastic data. In addition to its applications in experimental biophysics, we found that the maximum entropy production approach can also be used to develop a detailed understanding of the dynamics of slow variables in fast-rate processes. In the context of the Hodgkin-Huxley model, for example, we have successfully determined the time-evolving distribution of voltages across the cell membrane. This achievement marks the first time this level of detailed information has been obtained from the Hodgkin-Huxley model. In general, we found that the maximum entropy production approach can be used to develop a precise description of the dynamics of slow variables in fast-rate processes. In particular, this method returns the expected time-evolving distribution of the voltages across the cell membrane as output. Existing methods that address bias in high-dimensional settings typically rely on prior information or enhanced assumptions. However, due to their simplicity and versatility, minimal loss methods have become a preferred approach despite their well-documented drawbacks. This work aims to resolve the trade-offs associated with minimal loss methods by combining them with an innovative strategy for selectively addressing biased predictors. The proposed technique, dubbed inceptive minimal loss, can be applied using only first-order information without necessitating frequency-basis selection or increased constraints. Theoretical justifications validate the proposed method, highlighting its superior performance over traditional minimal loss methods in terms of both bias correction and control over optimization complexity. The inceptive minimal loss method's efficacy is demonstrated through simulations and data from the COVID-19 Medical Conversation Dataset, providing substantial improvements over current methods. The associated code can be accessed on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/tcl9876/IML.  The trade-offs inherent to minimal loss methods, particularly their tendency to overly penalize certain predictors, can significantly diminish their performance in selectively addressing biased predictors. This limitation is compounded in high-dimensional settings where minimal loss methods' efficacy largely relies on the relative sparsity of the biased predictors. To mitigate these drawbacks and facilitate a more effective balance between bias correction and optimization complexity, this work introduces the inceptive minimal loss (iML) method. The iML algorithm involves an innovative strategy for selectively addressing biased predictors by dynamically reconfiguring the minimal loss optimization objective. This reformulated objective incorporates a non-decreasing, first-order accessible penalty term, thereby promoting inceptive optimization towards the desired unbiased solution. Theoretical justifications provide a framework for the iML algorithm's convergence, while simulations and real-world data analyses reveal superior bias correction and generalization capabilities compared to traditional minimal loss methods. For instance, in high-dimensional, randomly generated datasets, the iML algorithm demonstrated up to 3.7 times superior performance in correcting selectivity bias. Similarly, in analyzing the COVID-19 Medical Conversation Dataset, the iML method yielded 0.02 improved correlation coefficients compared to the standard minimal loss approach. The OT problem is inherently convex, but solving it efficiently is challenging even for small input sizes due to its high computational complexity. A similar issue arises in using kernel-based methods, which significantly increase the problem's size and complexity. In an attempt to overcome these challenges, we propose a new convolutional OT coupling approach based on a low-rank kernel representation, which draws inspiration from the low-rank approximation in linear algebra. This novel method reduces the dimensionality of the kernel matrix by sampling input inputs using a random point set, then projecting the resulting function onto a set of convolutional kernel basis functions. The resulting convolutional OT coupling has a more compact and efficient representation, which can be computed quickly and accurately using randomized and pyramidal solver techniques. As a result, our method facilitates a wide range of applications in machine learning, where solving OT coupling efficiently was previously a major hurdle. Experimental results show that our low-rank convolutional OT coupling provides a stable and efficient solution with high accuracy, both in its weighted average and soft assignment variants. Furthermore, we developed a new supervised learning framework for OT coupling, which achieves state-of-the-art performance when trained with our new convolutional OT coupling. Against this backdrop, we propose a new statistical method - the matrix exponential spline (MES) - a nonparametric approach capable of providing estimators for the covariance matrix of MTS that can automatically accommodate changing properties and dynamic relationships over time. The proposed method features two associated splines: the first generates mature, stable covariance matrices, while the second provides estimates of the inverse of the covariance matrix, specifically the conditional cross-section mean, conditional on the time index. Theoretical proof of the "root-$n$" consistency of the MES is achieved by applying estimation tools for the Euclidean space of matrix-exponential functions, a previously under-explored topic. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation studies and a real-world case example from the Twitter platform, specifically in identifying popular hashtags and negative sentiment trends surrounding the MeToo movement in 2017. If we consider that these X-ray emissions could be similar to observations of powerful local galaxies like Circinus and Centaurus, then their hard X-ray spectrum should also reflect emission from the Anomalous O VI region. Therefore, we have carried out a high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy observation of the EGRG 0412+365 using the XMM-Newton, which allowed us to identify a narrow oxygen line. Our initial analysis indicates that the oxygen line has an energy of around 65.4 +/- 1.3 eV and the upper limit for its equivalent intensity is 1.5 x 10^42 erg/s/CM^2. Our data also reveal the presence of a broader 6.4 keV emission line with an equivalent intensity of approximately 2.2 x 10^38 erg/s/CM^2 and a 1 sigma uncertainty of 1.5 x 10^37 erg/s/CM^2. The soft X-ray spectrum we obtained is also noteworthy as it shows a consistent iron abundance and cooler gas temperature than previously thought, which may indicate the presence of a warm gas across the entire EGRG system. Our findings confirm that the X-ray emission mechanism of these powerful EGRGs can indeed be explained by not only synchrotron radiation from cosmic rays but also by thermal emission from the Anomalous O VI region, much like in the local galaxies Circinus and Centaurus. If every EGRG were to exhibit this thermal component then it could account for a previously unexplained 10% share of the 6.4 keV emission flux in the entire extragalactic X-ray spectrum. The X-ray emission mechanism of these powerful EGRGs can thus be explained by a combination of both leptonic and hadronic processes. Our data also set an upper limit for the charge exchange reaction between hydrogen and oxygen, which is consistent with the expectations of two-sided symmetry and not greater than 2.4 x 10^-14 cm^-2. Our proposed adaptation of Nonvolatile Memory (NVM) technology in base stations is an example of the latter. However, legal restrictions and data protection regulations often hinder a combined analysis of multiple such datasets. This paper presents a fully automated approach to link such datasets with a common identifier, even when addresses are involved. The method considers that a significant proportion of ties between individuals are plausible and uses these probabilities to automatically determine relevant connections. As a result, the method requires minimal user input and can typically be completed within a few hours or days, depending on the size of the data. The method has been successfully tested on two publicly accessible datasets and meets the highest security standards. The method is open-source, available at https://github.com/popgen-de/ddaddress-v2. The provided example use cases illustrate the wide range of applications possible when combining individual-level data from various sources. The additional benefit of using address data for data protection purposes is that users can remain anonymous while still gaining valuable insights from the combined data. This is achieved by first splitting one dataset and linking the remaining parts to the other dataset, and then randomly dispersing the individual records while maintaining essential relationships within the combined data. This new approach is called address-based fusion and - unlike existing methods - does also not require any information about individual ties within the data. Address-based fusion makes it possible to conduct a combined analysis while still respecting individual data protection if at least one of the involved parties maintains a degree of anonymity. The method has been carefully designed to be secure, efficient and flexible: secure, as it meets legal requirements and protects sensitive individual data; efficient, as it is based on an established technique; and flexible, as it can be applied in a range of contexts. The provided source code is open to feedback and can be used as a starting point for future research in the field of data fusion. The associated user study showed that the method is acceptable to its subjects, as it is based on commonly applied data protection regulations in the field. One major concern for the application of data fusion is the risk of data leakage - where combined data is shared with third parties, revealing individual identities. However, as the method is based on fully anonymous data, this risk is completely eliminated. However, as an alternative, the method called address-based fusion has been introduced, which is also open to feedback and can be used in various studies to combine data while maintaining a higher degree of anonymity. In our study, we demonstrate that any function mapping a set of feature means to a scalar can be approximated by conditioning on the individual feature values in a set of equations. We refer to this as the mean to marginalisation principle. While initially appearing as a logical consequence rather than a discovery, this finding turns out to be a powerful tool with far-reaching implications, allowing us to establish the instability of mean-aggregators, a type of machine learning model that predicts a variable based on the means of the training data's features. Indeed, combining the mean to marginalisation principle with a classic mathematical technique shows that there are infinitely many inputs on which mean-aggregators can be arbitrarily mistaken. Furthermore, our findings encompass not only the specific case of aggregators aggregating features, but also scenarios in which variables are predicted based on the means of a subset of the training data's features, as well as scenarios in which variables are conditioned on other variables. We show that there are infinitely many inputs on which mean-aggregators can produce incorrect outputs. Building upon this same approach, we also demonstrate that there are infinitely many inputs on which classifying the labels of data given the raw values is possible, but classifying the labels given their means is not. Notably, our approach does not rely on the distribution of the data and can be adapted to any function mapping a set of feature means to a scalar. In contrast to previous studies, which analyzed the stability of a specific distribution using specific estimators, our approach is distribution-agnostic and can be used with any function. We believe that exploring the limits of which functions can be reliably represented, what factors affect their stability, and what mathematical techniques are required to establish these limits can provide a deeper understanding of machine learning. In particular, our study sheds new light on the stability of mean-aggregators, a class of models that are increasingly popular but are now shown to be unstable on an infinite number of inputs. In terms of practical applications, our study suggests that data analysts may want to prioritise predicting the raw values of the data rather than its means, and may want to consider developing methods that are not dependent on aggregators. One potential avenue is to develop methods that are more stable and less susceptible to errors, such as classifiers that classify the labels of data given the mean values. To date, we still know very little about the limits of aggregation, and further research is clearly required

A notable question within this field, the P versus NP$\^*$ problem, has gone unsolved for decades; this conjecture proposes that the P class is essentially the inverse of the NP class, which can be obtained by restricting the allowed inputs to probabilistic circuits to have a zero output probability. Although NP$\^*$ encompasses various complex function classes including NP, P-NP, and more, the relationship between these classes is still largely unknown. In this paper, the first in-depth exploration of circuit complexity theory, we examine the background and recent advancements related to the P versus NP$\^*$ problem; this study focuses on translating non-deterministic Turing machine decision problems into circuit constraints via closure properties. Additionally, we provide cut-set expansion theorems that offer new insights into the complexity of functions computed by non-deterministic circuits with specific constraints. These results can serve as the groundwork for future research to refine our understanding of the hierarchy among NP, P-NP, P NP, and P$\^$. This particular installment specifically discusses the inaugural findings derived from the off-axis path scans of second-generation Telescopes I-IV. These path scans enabled the assessment of camera performance, optical quality, and mechanical robustness across the full 64 degree field of view. Using these path scans, the scanning strategy employed, and the resultant tracking data, we have calculated the angular resolution achievable by each of the four telescopes. This resolution ranges from 22 arcseconds to 45 arcseconds at energy thresholds of 100 GeV to 10 TeV. Moreover, the article highlights the project's full-publication open-access policy, as well as the growing repository of observational records and other scientific data made accessible by the project. Our analysis focuses on the system's phase space, comprised of the collective
configuration and momentum variables of the lattice's sites, and we establish
criteria for the system to exhibit two key properties: its completeness,
enabling the reversal of its time-evolution and realization of its natural
symmetries; and Lyapunov function existence, leading to the system being
classified as stable and dissipative. In particular, we demonstrate that when
the system is defined on a lattice with periodic boundary conditions and its
Hamiltonian is finite, its energy is confined to a bounded range and the
system displays distinct behavior in equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium
scenarios. Moreover, we show that infinite-range Hamiltonians result in the
loss of Lyapunov function existence but lead to the formation of homogenized
equilibrium states that exhibit periodic patterns. Our study includes a
comprehensive review and discussion of the concept of Lyapunov functions in the
context of multi-site many-body systems, as well as an exploration of the
concept's connection to thermodynamic principles. Our work has the potential to
inspire new areas of research in the fields of non-equilibrium physics and
condensed matter physics. In the supplementary materials, we delve into the
application of a Stackel matrix method, enabling the derivation of explicit
Lyapunov functions for multi-banded systems that possess symmetries, effectively
facilitating the identification of stable, infinite-range transport processes. 
These findings may pave the way for the creation of novel, non-equilibrium
phases in multi-banded systems, potentially leading to the design of systems
capable of analyzing time-evolving data and expediting information transport. 
In line with this, we propose a physical realization of these ideas through the
use of spin-1 bosons, capable of efficiently transporting a single bit of
information in non-equilibrium settings. Our study has a comparative analysis

have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing their ability to model complex relationships between inputs and outputs.  However, a significant challenge arises from the need for a vast amount of data to train and refine the network.  This requirement proves particularly problematic when utilizing CSI as input, given its inherent noise and resulting signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) issues.  Our solution proposes a method to address this issue by implementing a technique called knowledge distillation.  Initially, a more complex network is trained with readily available data, with the results transferred to a smaller, target network via the distillation approach.  This process enables the target network to quickly learn the relationships between inputs and outputs using the results provided by the more complex network as a guide.  This results in a significant reduction in the need for additional, noise-free training data for localization purposes, thereby addressing the inherent noise and resulting low SNR problem present in CSI.  Our approach was evaluated using the CSI localization technique, with resulting 4.4 meters accuracy located in a single optimization step after receiving the distillation results.  In comparison, similar deep network approaches required 200,000 training iterations to achieve 1.1 meters accuracy, but with the results obtained after receiving the distillation results, an 88% reduction in required iterations is seen. This problem has been given considerable attention recently in the context of adversarial learning, where the teacher is typically an adversary that labels examples to confuse the learner. 

  Our work presents a new framework for active learning that accounts for the teacher's and learner's objectives. We establish two key interaction types. The first, known as equalising interactions, involve labeling examples from a dataset where multiple samples are labelled by the teacher and classified correctly. A key vulnerability arises from the unchecked transmission of file patch metadata during the update process, which was previously unknown and unaddressed. Our research introduces a novel attack vector involving the manipulation of file patch metadata transmitted over HTTPS, exploiting the fact that client devices apply this data to local files. As a result, when a legitimate update is received, the applied patch can be inserted into a differing file, essentially turning the received patch into a zero-day exploit, with the added benefit of leaving behind minimal residual evidence. Our study highlights the importance of protecting file metadata during the update process and presents several techniques for abusing this vulnerability. To this end, we suggest that file metadata be randomized or hashed before the update is processed, and further emphasize the benefits of regularly updating file signatures. Our provided proof-of-concept code serves as a demonstration of this vulnerability and its potential ramifications, along with an evaluation of existing vulnerability exploitation tools. for prior knowledge and without storing any information from previous audio

We examined the fundamental characteristics of these ecosystems as well as the interactions between their constituent parts.  By applying a holistic approach and in-depth analysis, we were able to identify key factors that contribute to the flourishing of open-source ecosystems.  By comparing similar conditions between the two communities and the limited availability of financial resources, we were able to pinpoint the crucial role of community leadership in the success and growth of open-source ecosystems.  To further understand the resilience of these ecosystems, we conducted a cross-cultural in-depth study of the open-source movement in Brazil and both communities in Iceland.  To explore the potential for replication, we analyzed the similarities and disparities between the open-source movement and the AFM user community, ultimately suggesting ways for the latter to replicate the success of the former.  Conclusions: By developing open, transparent and inclusive collaborative frameworks, the Quantified Self and nanocellulose communities have achieved innovative breakthroughs.  Our comparative study of these ecosystems allowed us to identify the key factors that contribute to their success.  By shedding light on the importance of leadership in the initial stages of these ecosystems, we were able to provide practical advice for the AFM user community to replicate the success of its counterparts.  Our research revealed considerable potential for the AFM user community to thrive, urging researchers to further explore and replicate the shared characteristics of successful open-source ecosystems.  Ultimately, this study sought to provide invaluable insights and guidance that can aid researchers working to establish similar collaborative ecosystems centered around open platforms. Initially, the basic principles of programmability are outlined and then experimental results from a specific micromaser setup are presented. These experiments involved directing a microwave pulse through the micromaser, which resulted in the generation of a reliable single-photon state. Additionally, the study shows that the micromaser's output can be manipulated on-demand using a control pulse to produce a specific quantum state that represents a coherent combination of multiple possible states. This programmability is made possible by the micromaser's ability to store a large number of excited states in the transition zone, where the population of the excited states can be intentionally changed by the control pulse. Furthermore, the study shows that the programmable single-photon generation can be successfully combined with the quantum memory function of the micromaser to produce a controlled single-photon sequence. This programmatic control over the single-photon state is verified through the application of a control pulse, which retrieves the desired quantum state from the micromaser's memory. This study of the programmable single-photon source with optical micromasers showcases an innovative approach to quantum optics that sets it apart from conventional approaches using atomic ensembles, transmon qubits, or superconducting cavities. This research identifies the micromasers as promising candidates for implementing novel quantum information technologies. In contrast to microwave photons, the study also demonstrates the feasibility of generating programmable optical photons using Raman microlasers. This potential is highlighted by the possibility of performing quantum optics experiments similar to those using atoms or ions but with the added benefit of easier integration with optoelectronics. Finally, the study explores some potential applications of the programmable single-photon source by investigating coherent optical cat states and the observation of quantum phase transitions using non-ablative sampling. This research also identifies another possible application of the programmable microwave photons by demonstrating the use of quantum teleportation to transfer the state of a coherent photon to a distant location using a entangled pair of photons as the medium. This achieves a record-breaking teleported distance of 1.3 meters using only a single entangled pair of photons as the medium. This study showcases the feasibility of teleporting a coherent photon over a macroscopic distance using a programmable quantum optical teleporter. In conclusion, the study identifies the programmable single-photon source as a highly versatile quantum optics platform with a bright future in exploring novel quantum optics phenomena and applications. To overcome these limitations, a key strategy is to integrate quantum circuits into a broader classical control system that can adapt to changing circuit performance. However, most classical control systems are tailored to specific quantum targets and therefore often fail to effectively support NISQ devices. To address this issue, we present CLASIQUA, an open-source framework aimed at enabling the rapid design of modular classical control systems capable of efficiently integrating with NISQ devices. CLASIQUA's key strength lies in its ability to be scaled up to increasingly complex quantum devices, both in terms of the complexity of the quantum circuits and the duration of the associated classical control processes. CLASIQUA's source code is available under an open-source license, with a publicly accessible web-based interface supporting its functionality. In this paper, we introduce CLASIQUA, outlining its underlying principles, its user experience, and providing a case study of its application to the control of a NISQ device. From a computational perspective, a key method of achieving scalability is utilizing the MapReduce programming model. However, the high latency associated with synchronous map and reduce tasks can hinder system performance. To resolve this issue, researchers have developed asynchronous MapReduce algorithms. This paper presents an innovative solution, AMR++, a high-performance asynchronous MapReduce framework, designed to handle real-time data processing on contemporary CPU architectures. We have enhanced the basic asynchronous MapReduce algorithms in several ways. We have also developed a method to prevent unnecessary interruptions during the parallel execution of tasks, and we have chosen fine-grained preemption as the new task scheduling policy. This contribution marks the first iteration of the AMR++ framework, marking an important achievement in the development of efficient asynchronous MapReduce algorithms. In recent years, deep learning has achieved significant success in improving system performance, yet it has been largely overlooked as a tool for developing energy-efficient systems. In contrast, our proposed context-based data compression technique combines the benefits of data representation learning and efficient information storage. This approach involves learning essential context information from prior training data and applying a simple entropy-based compression scheme to yield a high compression ratio. Moreover, our novel neural architecture combines a transiformer and a convolutional neural network and yields a high quality of reconstructed data while minimizing information loss. Experimental results indicate that our technique can reduce system energy consumption by 50% or more without compromising performance. This outcome makes our method particularly suitable for resource-constrained devices, such as mobile phones, that require large amounts of data processing and analysis. In addition to data compression, our technique can also be used for data sketch generation and similarity retrieval to enhance system efficiency. This may involve reducing storage requirements for originally uncompressed data or enabling efficient similarity retrieval after data decomposition. Ultimately, our technique has the potential to be adapted to a range of other system design challenges to promote energy-efficient operation. This research outlines our experience in developing an energy-efficient system using context-based data compression. In contrast to prior studies, we have introduced a transiformer-based convolutional neural network for high-quality compression. In addition to our core technique, we also investigate the feasibility of data retrieval and similarity search to reduce system energy consumption. This research is enabled by our neural compression method, which allows direct access to compressed data and supports efficient retrieval and similarity search. This study is the first to adopt deep learning for data retrieval and similarity search on compressed data. A few attempts have been made to develop tree-based models, which are inherently interpretable, for image classification tasks; however, these efforts have been hindered by several limitations.  For example, the decision-making process in each branch is typically independent, which makes it difficult for models to leverage correlations between different image features.  Furthermore, the potential of feature synergies is underutilized in the decision-making process.  To address these challenges, we have proposed a novel tree-based deep neural network that combines the advantages of neural networks and decision trees.  Our model can seamlessly transfer knowledge between different decision-making branches through cross-tree feature interactions.  To facilitate more efficient information exchange, we have developed a technique for unlocking hidden relationships between decision-making branches.  Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model is highly efficient and can achieve superior performance with significantly reduced parameters compared to existing tree-based and non-tree-based networks.  Importantly, our model's decision-making process is equally accurate in classifying and explaining task-specific sub-populations as its competitor networks; however, the model's interpretability is notably higher due to its reduced parameter count and simpler architecture.  Our proposed model was evaluated on two medical image classification datasets, where it was shown to outperform PyTorch's default implementation of ResNet50 and SqueezeNet, as well as other tree-based networks on certain tasks.  Our code and dataset are publicly available for download at https://github.com/chenwen0809/CTNN.  Our proposed model is equally effective in classifying and explaining task-specific sub-populations and has notable advantages in parameter efficiency compared to state-of-the-art networks.  Our main contribution is a novel tree-based deep neural network that combines the strengths of tree and neural models for interpretable medical image classification.  Our model can seamlessly transfer knowledge between decision-making branches through cross-tree feature interactions and unlock hidden relationships between decision-making branches due to its high-parameter efficiency.  Our model is shown to achieve high accuracy on certain tasks with reduced requirements for model parameters and complexity.  Our model's decision-making process is equally accurate in classifying and explaining task-specific sub-populations as its competitor networks; however, the model is notably more interpretable due to its reduced parameter count. This serves as the basis for an alternative definition of recursive distributional dichotomous relations using Markov chains. This new approach allows us to define and study non-autonomous recursive distributional dichotomous relations. Importantly, it provides access to tools for examining the Fredholm properties of these relations and enables discussion of non-autonomous generalized resolvents. As a result, we are able to extend the definition of modes to non-autonomous Markov chains. Moreover, for any non-autonomous Markov chain satisfying certain conditions, we show that its stationary modes can be associated with a non-autonomous recursive distributional dichotomous relation. This is related to another area of interest: the extension of autonomous weak modes to non-autonomous Markov processes. In order to compare the two concepts, we establish a correspondence between non-autonomous and autonomous modes through the use of phase functions. However, as shown in an accompanying study, it is possible for non-autonomous phase functions to exhibit behavior that is similar to autonomous phase functions, provided that the associated non-autonomous system is closed. For instance, we obtain the closed system by imposing action-integrality on the non-autonomous kernel. As a consequence of this, we are able to extend the principles of the Lyapunov-Ford theorem to non-autonomous systems that are closed. This enables us to study the ergodic properties of these systems more deeply. Importantly, for any closed non-autonomous Markov chain, we show that its stationary modes can be associated with a phase function. This function in turn allows us to define the generalized Laplacian and study the eigenvalue problem of the non-autonomous system. As a result of this work, we are able to identify the critical features of phase functions associated with stationary modes in non-autonomous and autonomous Markov processes. This is true even in cases where the Markov processes are not ergodic. For instance, we are able to define the concept of weak stationary modes in non-autonomous Markov processes that are not ergodic. This is related to another area of interest: the extension of autonomous complete monotonicity to non-autonomous systems. Our new language, Jicochess, is a concurrent programming language that targets parallel scripts executed in JavaScript-like environments.  Jicochess integrates the concept of nested attributes within object-based threads (called 'chess pieces') to support the declaration and use of high-level, abstract functions across concurrent operations.  Its main features include the declaration of high-level functions within classes (called 'chess pieces'), a dynamic execution environment that balances scheduling, synchronization, and conflict resolution, and also incorporates error handling through piece-specific execution failures.  Jicochess is implemented using the Node.js ecosystem, allowing for the seamless integration of various libraries and tools.  A thorough evaluation of Jicochess was conducted through the creation of seven benchmark scripts, which demonstrate its performance in scenarios involving waiting, synchronization, exception handling, and complex concurrency operations.  Our experiments indicate that Jicochess successfully achieves a 61% reduction in overall code length, 52% improvement in performance complexity, 66% boost in concurrency levels, and also enables the implementation of diverse synchronization methods using a 70% reduction in code length.  A comprehensive comparison of Jicochess with existing concurrent programming languages also highlights its key features and functionality.  A full implementation of Jicochess along with its associated benchmark scripts is publicly available for download at  https://github.com/masdotjp/jicochess.  Our language has also been formally proven correct through the use of existing Jafra theorem provers, which identify and resolve potential runtime errors within the benchmark scripts.  This formal proof of correctness also enables the identification of improvement opportunities for the Jicochess compiler, leading to the detection of two potential bugs within the original implementation.  By retooling the benchmark scripts using the Jicochess translator, high-quality concurrent C code is generated, representing a major breakthrough in translating abstract, high-level concurrent programs into efficient, low-level machine code.  This innovative solution has the potential to significantly simplify the lower-bound interface between high-level programming languages and their corresponding machine code, thus reducing potential errors.  Our study also explores the application of Jicochess in translating scripts from multiple high-level programming languages into concurrent, distributed Java code suitable for execution on distributed systems.  Specifically, a Java driver and its accompanying database interface are employed in the translation process.  Our distributed code is successfully compiled from the target high-level programming languages,

Specifically, for any positive integer n greater or equal to 3, we construct a weighted planar graph with n vertices and a connected simple graph with n-1 vertices, both of which are isospectral. Moreover, we show that for every such n, the mentioned graphs are obtained by adding an appropriate edge to an eigenmatrix of their spectral measure. Furthermore, for n equal to 4 or 5, we provide additional examples of isospectral planar graphs that are not isospectral when considering all possible weightings. These examples are obtained using a novel method involving the construction of new graphs from old ones by replacing vertices with appropriate matrices. In addition, for every n greater or equal to 3, we show that the class of all isospectral planar weighted graphs with n vertices contains a subgroup of positive index, depending on the irreducibility of the characteristic polynomial of its spectral measure's eigenmatrix. If the spectral measure is irreducible, we give an explicit description of the obtained subgraph, while for the reducible case we specify a parameter and provide an example of a weighted graph that achieves the positive index for a specific parameter. Finally, for every n greater or equal to 3, we show that the existing methods of constructing isospectral graphs are unable to guarantee the production of such planar graphs for large n. Current methods for tackling this challenge mainly rely on epigraphical learning, where a stream of granular knowledge is combined to form a evolving granular space of concepts. However, these approaches only consider individual tasks' contribution to concept formation, neglecting the influence of individual data points. Moreover, existing frameworks restrict the representation of data concepts to Euclidean space, which may not be sufficient for some real-world data, particularly those with non-linear relationships. To address these limitations, we develop a new framework called the Hypergrano CL framework, which represents data concepts as hyper-spheres, utilizing hyper-spherical projections for pattern recognition. A novel hypergrano space, where each point represents a pattern classifier projecting data points' distributions onto the surface of their respective spheres, is explored as a streaming concept classifier. To tackle the challenge of avoiding memory retention from previous tasks, we employ weakly interpolative updating followed by hypergrano adaptation, along with a mechanism for selectively remembering significant data from previous tasks. Experimental findings demonstrate the efficacy and superiority of our proposed framework in tackling the problem of continual learning of a stream of tasks where each task comes with a class-labeling dataset. increasing use of smartphones and connected devices like smart home gadgets and vehicles.  Providing quality service to such traffic while keeping network air quality clean is an extremely challenging task.  Although this issue affects many networks, some specific technologies like Wi-Fi and Wi-Fi Direct encounter unique difficulties in managing traffic.  The problem becomes even more complicated by the presence of multiple traffic streams and the limited capacity for these technologies.  Due to their close relationship with each other, it is essential to find a harmonious balance in managing traffic among them.  This paper aims to address this challenge by proposing traffic allocation algorithms for managing Wi-Fi and Wi-Fi Direct's network traffic.  The paper introduces a new stream priority class to ensure critical streams have priority, and uses channel allocation and power management to optimize traffic capacity.  It performs traffic allocation in a sequence of steps - first identifying priority streams and identifying non-overlapping channels, then reordering non-IEEE 802.11ad streams by priority, and finally assigning power to IEEE 802.11ad to maximize capacity.  The paper reviews existing traffic management techniques, but unlike them, our proposal uses a single optimization technique.  The paper also confirms the effectiveness of our traffic allocation proposal with simulation results showing an 82% average improvement in network capacity for mixed traffic and an 88% average improvement for pure Wi-Fi Direct traffic.  The paper submitted this proposal to the IEEE 802.11ad group but did not receive a response. an online social media platform can help explain its remarkable resilience in the face of increased connectivity due to viral growth. However, the prevailing theories, specifically the scale-free hypothesis and the homophilic hypothesis, have drawn controversy in recent times. This study investigates the core composition of a massive online network with over 33 million users across more than 21 industries by examining the dynamics of community structure using the Modulated Matrix Product State algorithm. The analysis reveals that the core of the network does not adhere to either the scale-free or homophilic hypothesis. Alternatively, the study presents an alternative explanation for the core's formation by incorporating both internal and external linkages. The discovered architecture, characterized by a mixture of large in- and out-degrees within industry groups, raises important implications for the design of robust social networks. The findings provide valuable insights for the core components of social media platforms. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of the Modulated Matrix Product State algorithm is demonstrated through a comparison with the core-periphery model. The study concludes by outlining potential future research directions based on the underlying mechanisms of social media platforms. The study provides and visualizes the core community results for each industry on a dedicated website: csn.isi.ucla.edu/. The raw community structures and core identification code are available on GitHub: github.com/jase-clarkson/MMPS. The core identification code has been integrated into a larger GitHub project for social media analysis: github.com/jase-clarkson/SMA. The website will serve as a long-term reference for any changes to the core community structures over time, enabling researchers to validate the core identification model and analyze the dynamics of the online social media platform. The study also investigates the core community structures of four businesses on social media: Facebook, Twitter, Reddit, and Pinterest. The results reveal that the core of both Facebook and Twitter are characterized by a mixture of large in- and out-degrees within industry groups. The other two platforms display a primarily internal linking mechanism. The study provides key insights into social media architecture that can inform design choices, ranging from prioritizing viral growth to mitigating the spread of misinformation. The study shows that the core of social media platforms can be influenced by both internal and external linkages, with internal linkages appearing in industries dominated by user interactions and external linkages appearing in platforms with significant non-Industry user interactions. The study raises important implications for social media platforms, particularly those with primarily internal linkages, where the spread of misinformation can be amplified by the core community's ability to generate content.

around the young star V2775 SGR is caused by a circumstellar disc that has been photo-dissipated by the star's intense radiation.  V2775 SGR is a star in the final stages of its T-Tauri phase, and its dust-free disc is unusually large, at 83 au in radius.  Although we couldn't detect a dust disc, we were able to detect a warm circumstellar disc with a radius of 7.4 au using ALMA's spectral and temporal data.  Our models show that a very high luminosity from the star would require an extremely thin disc to avoid being detectable with ALMA's sensitivity, and thus we conclude that the disc cavity around V2775 SGR is most likely caused by its intense radiation.  Our findings also indicate that the disc's upper surface, exposed to the star's radiation, is likely to be almost completely gas-free.  Observations of this gas would allow us to study its temperature and composition, and potentially estimate the amount of gas in the disc cavity.  Furthermore, our findings suggest that radiation from V2775 SGR, with a spectral class of at least B9, is sufficient to prevent the formation of a stable dust disc, and this could have implications for the classification of other stars in the region.  Finally, our findings also suggest that the formation of planets in this system may be possible, and this could explain the observed properties of the orbiting planet.  Our findings further reveal that very low-mass objects, down to the mass of Kuiper belt objects, may be released from the disc during its lifetime, and these objects could potentially be detected with future technology.  Our study of V2775 SGR therefore offers insights into the development of planetary systems, particularly those that are exposed to very high levels of radiation.  At the same time, its development is also comparable to other stars in the region, such as MWC 480, which have lower radiation strengths.  Further study of these stars could lead to a better understanding of this phenomenon. It may also be possible to observe objects of low mass that are released from the disc during its lifetime with future technology, such as in the case of V2775 SGR and other similar systems. Our focus is on identifying graphs whose quantum walk queries require a significantly lower number of iterations in comparison to classical random walks. Specifically, this can be achieved either by diminishing the number of random queries needed for a given walk length or by reducing the walk length required for a certain number of queries. Building upon Szegedy's quantum walk framework, we introduce a general method for creating quantum circuits that incorporates an absorbing vertex to streamline our analysis. We then illustrate the applicability of this method through several examples showing that quantum walks can indeed be used more efficiently than classical random walks. Specifically, this is true for transitive graphs as well as bounded-degree graphs that are either expanders or have a specific structure requiring a large number of iterations. Furthermore, we show that quantum walks can also be used more efficiently than classical random walks on graphs whose diameter is constant, provided that the total number of vertices is extremely large. In our research, we present MAVE, a novel MARL algorithm designed for multi-goal environments that demand collaborative behaviors among multiple agents. MAVE stands out from other methods as it identifies and learns optimal network connections autonomously from observations rather than pre-defined structures. The results show that MAVE not only reduces communication overhead but also achieves better performance compared to state-of-the-art MARL algorithms. This study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of interdependent systems, focusing on core concepts, classification systems, evaluation criteria, mathematical foundations, and application use cases. Three methodologies for biclustering are presented along with corresponding examples and discussions of their strengths and limitations. In recent times, there has been an increasing interest in incorporating fairness as a key factor in system design. However, the concept of fairness is still evolving and there is no consensus on its optimal definition. As a result, different approaches to fairness have been developed, each with its own underlying assumptions and implications. This study aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the concept of fairness, focusing on its various operational definitions and information-based interpretations. It also introduces a general theoretical framework for fairness, grounded in logical reasoning, and examines the applications of fairness in practical contexts. In particular, this study investigates the relationships between fairness, uncertainty, randomness, and the principles of equality and equity. A distinction is made between procedural and substantive fairness, with an evaluation of their underlying principles and implications. A critical discussion on the most commonly used indicators of fairness is included, with an examination of their strengths and limitations. This study explores the possibilities of incorporating fairness into the development of artificial intelligence and machine learning models, with an emphasis on its relevance to interdependent systems. A final reflection on the future of fairness is provided, with recommendations for its continued development in this field. This paper presents CTAPO, a novel decentralized, peer-to-peer proximity detection framework. In comparison to existing solutions, CTAPO offers an unprecedented degree of user anonymity and privacy. Additionally, our research demonstrates that CTAPO can effectively identify nearby users with reduced accuracy variability, effectively mitigating exposure compensation factors, and can also accurately detect users within large environments. Our CTAPO framework has been successfully implemented and evaluated on various low-energy wireless processors. In addition to these processor-based tests, we have also conducted a large-scale simulation study to validate the CTAPO proximity detection capabilities in real-world scenarios. Simulation results have revealed a notable enhancement of up to 70% in the overall system's accuracy when compared to the best-performing individual method. Furthermore, the CTAPO contact tracing framework offers notable benefits in terms of privacy, with quantifiable reductions in risk values ranging from 75% to >99%, depending on the specific context. Our CTAPO contact tracing framework consists of three primary components: location unobfuscation, exposure compensation, and proximity detection. This framework is designed to be decentralized, with a user-centric philosophy, and provides the option for users to control the extent of contact tracing activity in their devices. In the event of a user choosing to support contact tracing, the location unobfuscation module anonymizes their location data while enabling extraction of proximity logs, which are then reported to public health authorities. The exposure compensation module compensates for situations where contact tracing alone is insufficient to identify exposures, while the proximity detection module uses received signal strength indicators to identify nearby users within large environments, effectively aiding public health authorities in containing outbreaks. As part of our peer-to-peer proximity detection framework, CTAPO leverages the study's previous research findings in decentralized contact tracing to accurately detect nearby users within various real-world settings, while also offering enhanced anonymity and privacy compared to existing contact tracing solutions. In addition to our CTAPO proximity detection framework's accuracy and energy efficiency, an open-source implementation has been made available on low-energy wireless processors, including the Advanced RISC MICS and TelosB platforms, for further research purposes. In the near future, the user-centric contact tracing app will be successfully implemented on these low-power wireless processors to further enhance our understanding of the CTAPO proximity detection framework's potential applications in real-world contact tracing scenarios. Program synthesis is the process of creating a program based on a given problem, typically by describing the desired program's behavior using test cases, positive examples, or mathematical expressions. In contrast, traditional human programming often relies on pre-existing code fragments, programming manuals, and problem-solving expertise passed down through years of experience. However, as programs grow in complexity, even expert human programmers struggle to fully comprehend their own code. As a result, the program synthesis field has seen numerous approaches that describe programs using simple building blocks, but these methods often overlook the essential role of human problem-solving expertise in linking these building blocks to their underlying problems. To address this gap, we introduce a new approach called "problem-linked abstractions," which facilitates program synthesis by linking high-level program abstractions with problem-specific attributes. Our system, called "Formulaic," uses a collaboration network that consists of both "formulaters" (experts who define problem-related attributes) and "implementers" (developers who link these attributes to executable code). By integrating these components, Formulaic can synthesize complex algorithms for real-world problems that defy synthesis via conventional methods. In particular, Formulaic was used to generate novel matrix multiplication algorithms, affine matrix multiplication, and permutohedron indexing, where the program schemes were defined by domain-specific attributes such as matrix layouts, indexing methods, and graph structures. Our evaluation demonstrates that Formulaic can produce more accurate and efficient programs than state-of-the-art program synthesizers, and its index generation capabilities outperform existing permutohedron indexing libraries by an order of magnitude. In addition, Formulaic's index generation has already led to the discovery of novel permutohedron indexing techniques and a more robust matrix multiplication algorithm. Our study shows that the potential of program synthesis can be fully realized only when the program scheme is described by problem-specific attributes devised by domain experts, and these attributes are linked to the underlying problems in a meaningful way. As such, the Formulaic framework serves as a powerful tool for human domain experts to collaborate with machine programmers, yielding high-quality programs that were previously impossible to synthesize using conventional methods. Furthermore, the abstract representations of the programs, which show the links between variables and attributes, provide valuable program documentation and also support program verification and testing. The simulations are conducted using a various range of impurity concentrations, from extremely rare to high frequency, in large systems sized 400x400 to 800x800. The impurities are represented by atoms of a second material with a mismatched lattice structure, from which 2D islands can form. The simulations are conducted under equilibrium conditions and impurity concentrations are calculated as a fraction of the maximum possible number of misfit dislocations. The nucleation process is studied under both thermodynamic conditions, driven by free energy minimization, and through time-dependent processes. The simulations reveal that the significant factors affecting nucleation behavior are system size, impurity concentration, and background properties. The results show that the nucleation behavior adheres to a log-normal distribution at large scales but follows a power-law pattern at a smaller level, with slopes highly correlated with concentration. Our analysis shows that the steady increase in entropy within closed systems is solidly based in the fundamental principles of symmetry, with the underlying symmetries determining the consequences for entropy when particles are involved.  By breaking down the complex interactions between particles and identifying the unique parts that contribute to entropy, we gain a deeper understanding of the fundamental principles of symmetry.  These principles dictate that the total entropy remains unchanged, but also reveal the local effects that contribute to the overall increase in entropy within closed systems.  These local effects, though fundamental and inevitable in closed systems, are often overlooked because they can also be seen as part of more extensive patterns when the system is not enclosed.  However, our focus on discrete entropic symmetries helps to pinpoint these local effects and their role in understanding entropy's increase over time.  By doing so, we provide a framework for validly measuring and interpreting entropy's increase in physical processes without relying on comparisons with thermodynamic perfection.  Furthermore, we identify a previously unexamined local effect, a form of entropic breakdown that occurs during the collision of two particles, characterized by a focused buildup of uncertainty in the collision partner's momentum.  This newly identified effect not only affects entropy's increase over time, but also reveals an accompanying small-scale, forward-focused focal point of momentum scattered from the primary collision target.  Similar entropic breakdowns likely exist for more intricate interactions, though calculating these more complex scenarios is a formidable task.  By recognizing the fundamental role of discrete entropic symmetries, we open the door to using entropy's increase over time as a powerful tool to gain insights into the intricate details of particle interactions.  In turn, this deeper understanding of the fundamental processes of nature may uncover novel perspectives on the origins of the universe and the intricate web of particle interactions that shape it.  In support of this work, we have created the Entropic Symmetry Explorer (ESE), a user-friendly digital tool, accessible at https://beyondcwimberly.github.io/ESE/, which allows individuals to explore the local effects contributing to the overall increase in entropy across various processes.  By making this tool publicly available, we hope the broader scientific community can contribute to understanding and improving it, accelerating progress in this field.  Ultimately, this will enable researchers to make more accurate predictions about the intricate details of particle interactions, a goal we refer to as Entropic Precision. Another notable difference between these two phrases lies in their origin - "black and white" is rooted in film, while "like night and day" is from literature. Today, it's commonly used to describe things that are clearly distinguished as being on one side or the other, whether that be in film, television, or elsewhere. This means that "black and white" is typically used for things that are clearly distinguished, whereas "like night and day" is used for things that are clearly distinct but not necessarily clearly different. Additionally, both phrases are clear examples of non-binary opposition, which is typically seen in metaphors and metaphysical discussions, as opposed to everyday, literal conversations. The everyday variation of this phenomenon is typically observed in binary opposition, which is clearly seen in phrases like "good and bad." This is why we might say that "black and white" is a clear spectrum, as opposed to night and day, which is a binary distinction. In summary, the phrases "like night and day" and "black and white" are used to describe clearly distinct things in this world, as opposed to each other.
